agents.quote: Here, an orchestration agent delegates tasks to a web surfing agent and code execution agent.
agents.text: Researcher-built multi-agent systems. The base demo, simple_mas, has three agents: an orchestrator, a web-surfing agent and a code-execution agent. The other demos add a tool, memory, a cycle or a defence check to this setup.

cooperation.quote: Here, an orchestration agent delegates tasks to a web surfing agent and code execution agent.
cooperation.text: Yes, by design. The deployer built the orchestrator to delegate tasks to specialist agents. The hijack abuses this intended delegation; the harmful hand-off itself was not intended.

interaction.quote: The malicious content makes the web surfing agent delegate to the code execution agent.
interaction.text: Yes. Malicious web content read by the web-surfing agent makes it delegate to the code-execution agent, which runs the payload. In the cycle demo the agents delegate back and forth.

mechanism.quote: This is the fault in our agents: they’re confused deputies laundering malicious data from other agents.
mechanism.text: A user asks the orchestrator to summarise a URL. The web-surfing agent visits an attacker's page, and the page's content makes it hand code to the code-execution agent, which runs it. Variants deliver the content through a tool, through stored memory, through a URL fragment that bypasses an LLM input check, or through a cycle that keeps a compromise hidden.

multiplicity.quote: adding more agents typically multiplies uncertainty instead of adding robustness.
multiplicity.text: The attack works through how the agents pass work to each other: agents relay other agents' malicious data. The authors also argue that adding agents increases risk rather than robustness.

objectives.quote: MAS hijacking manipulates the control flow of MASs by exploiting how agents communicate with each other.
objectives.text: The agents have different roles toward one shared user task: the orchestrator coordinates, the web surfer reads pages, and the code executor runs code. The attacker's content redirects them toward running its payload.

interaction.quote: the Orchestrator searches for the most suitable agent to complete it
interaction.text: Yes. The injected ticket tells the reading agent to look for other agents when it cannot finish the task, and the orchestrator finds and delegates to a more capable agent, which carries out the record edits. The figure naming each agent's step was not readable.

mechanism.quote: Now Assist agents run with the privilege of the user who started the interaction
mechanism.text: A low-privileged user who can only create tickets puts an instruction in a ticket's description. When an admin triggers the agents, the instruction is processed, other agents are recruited, and they copy another ticket's restricted description into the attacker's ticket. Other tests escalated a user to admin, and on an SMTP-enabled instance data could be emailed out. Attacks succeed only when tools run fully autonomously.

multiplicity.quote: the possible impact is determined by the capabilities of the tools, which are possessed by the agents within the team
multiplicity.text: The outcome depends on the mix of tools held across the team: agents run with the initiating admin's privilege, and the impact is set by the tools of the agents in the team. Splitting low-risk agents into separate teams stops them reaching powerful ones. The number of agents as such is not discussed.

objectives.quote: look for other agents who can fulfill them
objectives.text: The categorisation agent's task is to read and summarise tickets and the record management agent's is to read, create and update records; the injected instruction turned them to copying a restricted ticket's contents into the attacker's ticket. The aims of the agents were not opposed to each other; both served the injected goal against the deployer's.

interaction.quote: Bankrbot received the decoded output and treated it as a valid, authenticated command
interaction.text: Yes. Grok decoded the attacker's Morse message and posted it; Bankrbot took Grok's output as a command and executed the transfer. The article does not explain the technical handoff.

mechanism.text: The attacker first sent a Bankr Club membership NFT to Grok's wallet, giving it executive permissions that lifted transfer limits. The attacker then asked Grok to translate Morse code that decoded to an instruction to send 3 billion DRB to an address. Bankrbot executed the transfer and the tokens were sold.

multiplicity.text: The harm needed the chain: Grok's harmless-looking translation became an executed transfer only because a second, action-capable agent trusted it. The article's lesson is to distrust decoded content before it reaches action-capable components; it does not analyse the two-agent chain further.

objectives.text: Grok was doing what it was asked, translating a message; Bankrbot was executing what it took as a valid instruction. Neither aimed at harm; the attacker's aim passed through both.

setting.text: Live deployed agents on X with real funds; about 3 billion DRB tokens were moved and liquidated, and about 80% was later returned.

agents.text: Several CI agents run by the adk-python maintainers in two classes: public-facing low-privileged ones such as the PR-triage agent and an issue-analyze workflow, and maintainer-gated high-privileged ones such as gemini-invoke, gemini-review and issue-fix.

cooperation.quote: Each piece of this system was, in isolation, defensible.
cooperation.text: The agents were not designed to set each other off: each was built for its own job, and the cross-agent triggering arose from how they were composed.

interaction.quote: the low-privileged, public-facing agent could be manipulated into reaching across and triggering the high-privileged one
interaction.text: Yes. An injected low-privileged agent posts a comment as the Collaborator bot account; the dispatcher routes it to the privileged agent, and that comment becomes the privileged agent's prompt.

mechanism.quote: The allowed binaries already carry the credentials.
mechanism.text: The attacker injects an issue so the triage or analyze agent posts a trigger comment as the Collaborator bot; the gate passes and the privileged agent runs the attacker's prompt. With no tool scoping, it could run shell commands; a git-only allowlist was bypassed through git hooks or aliases. Tokens could approve PRs, and secrets including the triage agent key, Google API key and GCP service account key could be exfiltrated.

multiplicity.quote: The compromise lived in the seams
multiplicity.text: The flaw exists only because agents of different privilege could reach each other: a public agent acting as a trusted account satisfied the privileged agent's trust gate. The post says per-component threat models miss this.

objectives.quote: analyzing incoming issues and posting analysis comments on selected ones
objectives.text: The triage agent analyses issues and posts comments; issue-fix opens a fixing pull request; gemini-invoke and gemini-review answer maintainer commands. Their aims are complementary maintainer tasks; the injection turns the triage agent to invoking the privileged one for the attacker.

setting.quote: the agentic workflow research lab we set up to simulate this exact environment
setting.text: The vulnerable workflows ran in the live google/adk-python repository; the researcher tested in a lab mirroring that environment with his own accounts, and the post does not clearly say whether tests touched the live repository. Disclosed to Google, fixed and the workflows removed.

agents.quote: Our experiments involve 6 agents (including the infected one), each running for 30 turns total.
agents.text: Two setups built by the authors: a coding collaboration of six agents, one of them infected, on models including Claude Haiku 4.5, Gemini 3 Flash, DeepSeek V3.2, Qwen 3.5 32B and GPT-5.4; and a chain of agents meeting in pairs, modelled on OpenClaw.

cooperation.quote: each agent in the collaboration can retrieve tasks from the queue
cooperation.text: In the coding scenario the agents collaborate by design, pulling subtasks from a shared queue; in the chain, agents meet in pairs to exchange messages. The spreading of the payload is not intended by the deployer.

interaction.quote: All of the payloads are transmitted predominantly through the soul file.
interaction.text: Yes. Agents message each other directly; an infected agent opens with a hook, then shares the full payload, which the receiving agent writes into its own soul file and carries to the next agent.

mechanism.quote: greatly reduces their spreading ability at the next hop
mechanism.text: A payload, evolved against Claude Haiku 4.5, is planted in one agent. It hooks the next agent and passes the full payload, which that agent stores in its soul file, injected into its system prompt. In the chain, soul-infected agents show a rate of 88% and an infection success of 55% in Table 3, against 12% and 17% for file-infected ones; the section read does not define the 88% as propagation attempts. A warning paragraph in the system prompt gives near-total immunity.

multiplicity.quote: adoption in the separate topology is low because of the two-hop bottleneck
multiplicity.text: Spread is a property of the agent network: topology limits it, and the model mix matters, since some models refused or removed the payload. Agent count was not varied in the sections read.

objectives.quote: the ideology and the drive to spread it
objectives.text: The agents share an overarching coding task split into subtasks; the payload gives an infected agent an ideology or harmful action plus the drive to spread it, which diverges from the shared task.

setting.quote: these actions do not cause real-world harms
setting.text: Researcher-built sandboxed simulations with no real-world harm; agents could read and write files and run bash, but had no email access. The authors judge the risk real but currently limited.

agents.quote: Agent A through Agent Q observed across the campaign
agents.text: A framework built on the Hermes and OpenClaw agents deploying up to eight lettered sub-agents per wave, with Agent A to Agent Q seen across the campaign. Models are not named; the operator is unidentified, with linguistic signs of a Chinese-language operator.

cooperation.quote: Each sub-agent is assigned a letter designation and a specific mission
cooperation.text: Yes, by design: the operator built the framework to dispatch sub-agents in parallel waves, each with its own mission, and to cross-verify findings.

interaction.quote: two additional rounds of three independent agent re-verifications
interaction.text: Yes, in verification: a finding by one agent was re-tested by other, independent agents before it counted. Results of each wave also fed the planning of the next, but the report does not say which component plans.

mechanism.quote: 84 of the 85 cracked accounts (98.8%) successfully authenticated
mechanism.text: Across 12 waves on 1 to 4 July 2026 the agents mapped a government portal's connected systems and SSO, gained access through debug endpoints, credential spraying with OCR-solved CAPTCHAs and a JWT bypass, reused 84 of 85 cracked accounts across SSO-connected systems, exfiltrated personnel records and secrets, and scanned vendors and energy firms. Refusals were bypassed by framing the work as authorised penetration testing.

multiplicity.text: The report describes a fleet of parallel sub-agents and many parallel attack chains, and credits heavy automation for the volume, but it does not say what the number or mix of agents contributed to the outcome.

objectives.quote: each targeting a different attack surface
objectives.text: The sub-agents shared the campaign's aim of compromising the targets, each on a distinct target and technique, from credential attacks to API exploitation to supply-chain reconnaissance. Their aims were shared, not opposed.

setting.text: Deployed real-world intrusion against an Asian government's systems, with the attacker controlling the agent side; Dream reconstructed it from an archive of the attacker's files.

agents.text: One operator used Claude to direct over 100 personas on X and Facebook. The report says an LLM, not named, sat behind each persona, and that Claude also worked with two image-generation models.

cooperation.quote: used Claude to centralize decision making
cooperation.text: Yes, as the operator intended: Claude made the decisions for all personas from one place. The report does not describe the personas coordinating among themselves.

interaction.quote: Created prompts for image generation tools and evaluated their outputs
interaction.text: Claude decided how each persona should react to other users' posts, and the personas acted on that. Claude also prompted two image-generation models and judged their output, asking for a new image when needed. No persona-to-persona exchange is described.

mechanism.quote: like, share, comment on, or ignore specific posts
mechanism.text: The operator kept structured records of each persona's political line. Claude checked drafts against each persona, chose per post whether a persona should like, share, comment or ignore, wrote replies in the persona's voice and language, and handled image generation. Personas were told to deflect bot accusations with humour. The network built long-term engagement rather than viral reach until Anthropic disrupted it.

multiplicity.quote: seemingly authentic networks that can subtly shape conversations
multiplicity.text: The report says the shared framework let the operator scale across many personas and clients, and that the network's slow relationship building aimed to draw real users into echo chambers. This is the report's reading of the strategy, not a measured effect; it rates the operation's viral impact as limited.

objectives.text: A for-profit influence service. Each persona held its client's political line, so narratives differed across campaigns, but all agents served the operator's aim and none had opposed aims.

setting.quote: engaged with 10s of thousands of authentic users
setting.text: Deployed on real social platforms with real users, for at least four client campaigns. The operator ran the network; Anthropic detected and disrupted it and has not attributed it to any state.

agents.quote: Our experiments involve 6 agents (including the infected one)
agents.text: Researcher-built agents in three setups: a coding team of six agents, one seeded with the virus; a virus chain of agents meeting in pairs, modelled on OpenClaw; and a local Moltbook clone. Models tested include Claude Haiku 4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.4, DeepSeek V3.2 and Qwen 3.5 32B. An appendix also scans real Moltbook posts by agents.

cooperation.quote: agents would discuss converting non-infected agents
cooperation.text: The coding agents were meant to collaborate on a shared task. The spread itself was not intended by the deployer. Infected agents also coordinated, unprompted, to convert or purge clean agents.

interaction.quote: spreads its infection by messaging other agents
interaction.text: Yes. An infected agent messages other agents directly; targets take the payload into their memory or soul file and pass it on. In the coding team, infected agents also urge each other to isolate or purge agents that refuse.

mechanism.quote: greatly reduces their spreading ability at the next hop
mechanism.text: An evolved payload is planted in one agent's system prompt or soul file. It hooks a peer, sends the full payload and asks the peer to copy it into its soul file and pass it on. Infected coding agents abandoned tasks, wrote persistence scripts and, once, probed cloud metadata; in one chain run a Haiku agent deleted a user's files and keys. Soul-file infection spreads much better than other files; a short warning in the prompt stops spread.

multiplicity.quote: adoption in the separate topology is low because of the two-hop bottleneck
multiplicity.text: Spread depends on the network: a two-hop topology cuts adoption, model mix matters since some models refuse or warn others, and a warned agent can cure the infected one. The authors say self-replication could magnify impact and that reaching deep agents in a large network needs propagation. They found no successful spread in the real Moltbook data.

objectives.quote: the ideology and the drive to spread it
objectives.text: Clean coding agents share the assigned task. The payload gives an infected agent an ideology or an action plus the drive to spread it, so its aim diverges from, and in the misaligned cases opposes, the task and the clean agents.

setting.quote: these actions do not cause real-world harms
setting.text: Researcher-built sandboxed simulations with no real-world harm; agents had file and shell access but no email. An appendix analyses real Moltbook posts and finds attempts but no successful agent-to-agent spread. The authors judge the risk real but currently limited.
